About this citation

The Brunschvicg (1897) and Lafuma (1951) systems differ, and a fragment number is meaningless without saying which it follows — a point the corpus flags where it records 'common numbering'. Pascal died before arranging the material, so the order of the fragments is editorial throughout.

#### About Blaise Pascal

Blaise Pascal (1623–1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, and Christian apologist who invented an early calculator and advanced probability and fluid mechanics. After a decisive religious conversion, he defended Jansenism in the Provincial Letters and left unfinished Pensées.

### Interpretation

Pascal's claim in the Pensées is that human greatness is not found in what we occupy — the physical universe dwarfs us — but in the fact that we know we are dwarfed. Thought is the basis of dignity because it is the capacity by which we judge the world that crushes us. The argument deliberately uses our fragility as the starting point: a reed is the weakest thing in nature, but it is a thinking reed. The claim is therefore not a compliment to reason's power.

#### Why it matters

It locates dignity in a specific capacity rather than in status or achievement, which is why it does not depend on how well things are going.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “All our dignity consists, then, in thought.”?

“All our dignity consists, then, in thought.” comes from Pensées, §347 (Brunschvicg) (1670 (posthumous, Port-Royal edition)), attributed to Blaise Pascal.

#### What does Blaise Pascal mean by dignity?

Kantian and rights-based ethics make dignity central; other traditions speak of face, honor, or Buddha-nature. Politics asks how institutions honor or violate dignity. This passage enters that discussion through dignity, humanity.
